name: Seaweed wrap

card.summary: A spa treatment in which seaweed paste is applied to the body and covered, promoted for smoother, firmer, hydrated-looking skin and temporary slimming.
card.note: Temporary inch loss is from fluid; infections are reported in immunosuppressed patients.

quick.overview:
A seaweed wrap coats the body in a seaweed or algae preparation, often covered with bandages or plastic, in a spa or at home. Providers promote it for softer, more hydrated skin and a slimmer look.

It belongs to thalassotherapy, the use of seawater and sea products for wellbeing. Reported effects on size are temporary, and skin-feel benefits are mainly what spa clients describe.
quick.how: Treatments are done in spas: product is applied, the body is wrapped for a period, and then rinsed. Results people describe are short-lived and are often repeated as a series.
quick.risks: The FDA has described body-wrap inch loss as temporary, from fluid, and warned excessive fluid loss can cause dehydration. A case report describes a Mycobacterium marinum infection in a psoriasis patient on adalimumab after a seaweed wrap.

lead: A seaweed wrap, sometimes called a thalasso wrap, applies seaweed to the skin as part of a spa treatment, and is promoted for hydration, smoother skin and slimming.[1][2]

Thalassotherapy, the broader practice of using seawater and sea products, has roots in 18th century seaside therapy associated with Dr. Richard Russell, and Lydia Sarfati is credited with introducing seaweed skin treatments to the United States.[1]

Researchers and regulators describe wrap-related size loss as temporary. The FDA stated in 1982 that body wraps do not dissolve fat, and a 2017 case report documents an infection after a seaweed wrap.[2][3]

chain: Skin hydrated and temporary fluid loss
angle.text: Users get a short-term change in how skin looks and feels and in measurements. Providers also promote it as a relaxing spa step before events.

paras: Thalassotherapy's seaside bathing vogue in the second half of the 18th century is linked to Dr. Richard Russell, and heated saltwater baths became popular in the 19th century.[1]

Wikipedia notes there is no scientific evidence that thalassotherapy is effective.[1] On wraps generally, the FDA said in FDA Consumer (1982) that loss of inches from sweating is temporary and warned of potentially dangerous dehydration.[2]
A 2017 Dermatology Online Journal report describes M. marinum infection in a psoriasis patient treated with adalimumab, linked to a seaweed wrap.[3]
No studies found. The only published human report is a single case of infection after a seaweed wrap.[3]

timeline.event: FDA Consumer warns body-wrap loss is temporary.[2]
Case report of M. marinum infection after a seaweed wrap.[3]
